faq.a: Rupture shows a palpable gap and loss of extension with intact wrist extension; radial nerve palsy has wrist drop but the tendon remains intact.
faq.q: How can I tell a triceps tendon rupture from a radial nerve palsy?

faq.a: Because it crosses the shoulder joint, weakness may be evident when the patient resists shoulder extension or adduction.
faq.q: Why is the long head important for shoulder exams?

faq.a: Ask the patient to extend the thumb and index finger; inability indicates posterior interosseous involvement while sensation stays normal.
faq.q: What bedside test helps confirm posterior interosseous nerve injury?

exam: A patient presents with inability to extend the elbow after a fall – what is your next step? — Perform a focused elbow extension test and palpate for a tendon gap; if absent, assess radial nerve function.
How does a radial nerve lesion differ from a triceps tendon rupture on exam? — Tendon rupture shows a gap and preserved wrist extension; radial nerve lesion shows wrist drop with intact tendon.
What is the significance of the long head’s origin for shoulder pathology? — It means shoulder extension or adduction weakness may accompany triceps dysfunction, guiding a broader joint exam.

In a low‑resource setting without ultrasound, how would you confirm a triceps tendon rupture? — Rely on clinical signs: palpable defect, loss of active elbow extension, and comparison with the opposite arm.
What complications arise from untreated compartment syndrome of the posterior arm? — Irreversible muscle necrosis, permanent loss of elbow extension, and possible radial nerve damage.

Why might a patient with posterior interosseous nerve palsy retain normal sensation? — The posterior interosseous branch is purely motor; sensory fibers travel in the main radial nerve proximal to the branch.
Which vessels are at risk during surgical exposure of the triceps? — The profunda brachii artery and its perforating branches; careful hemostasis prevents hematoma.
How would you differentiate a triceps strain from a full‑thickness tear clinically? — Strain causes mild pain with resisted extension; a full‑thickness tear shows a palpable gap and marked weakness.
ai.title: Triceps Brachii Anatomy
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The triceps brachii is the primary elbow extensor, composed of three heads with distinct origins and a common insertion on the olecranon. Its neurovascular supply, relations, and common injuries are crucial for clinical assessment in low‑resource settings.

b: Three heads: long, lateral, medial
Primary elbow extensor
Assists shoulder extension (long head)
sections.p: The triceps brachii is a large, three‑headed muscle on the posterior arm that extends the forearm at the elbow and stabilises the shoulder joint.

b: Long head: scapular origin, crosses shoulder joint
Lateral head: proximal humerus, most superficial
Medial head: distal humerus, deepest
sections.p: The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, the lateral head from the posterior humeral shaft above the radial groove, and the medial head from the posterior shaft below the radial groove. All converge into a single tendon inserting on the olecranon process of the ulna.

b: Radial nerve in radial groove
Brachial artery lies medial to the muscle
sections.p: Anteriorly the triceps lies deep to the brachialis and brachioradialis. Posteriorly it is covered by the skin and subcutaneous tissue; the radial nerve runs in the radial groove between the lateral and medial heads.

b: Profunda brachii gives main perforating branches
Radial recurrent contributes to distal portion
sections.p: Supplied by branches of the profunda brachii artery (deep brachial) and the radial recurrent artery.

b: Radial nerve lesion → weak elbow extension
Posterior interosseous palsy spares sensation
sections.p: Innervated by the radial nerve (C6‑C8). The posterior interosseous branch supplies the lateral and medial heads; the long head receives fibers directly from the radial nerve before it bifurcates.

b: Elbow extension strength test: resisted straight‑arm push
Long head contributes to shoulder extension
sections.p: Extends the forearm at the elbow; the long head also assists in shoulder extension and adduction. During pushing actions, the triceps stabilises the elbow joint.

b: Triceps tendon rupture: palpable gap, inability to extend elbow
Radial nerve palsy: wrist drop, loss of triceps strength
Compartment syndrome of the posterior arm: pain, tense swelling
sections.p: Trauma, over‑use, and nerve injury can impair triceps function. In low‑resource settings, presentation may be limited to weakness without imaging.

t.b: Is triceps strength intact? – Weakness suggests tendon injury or radial nerve lesion
Visible gap or depression over olecranon indicates rupture
Normal sensation with weakness points to posterior interosseous branch injury

b: Ask patient to push against resistance with arm straight – assesses triceps power
Compare bilateral elbow extension to detect subtle weakness
Check radial nerve function (wrist extension) to differentiate nerve vs tendon problem
sections.p: Focus on functional testing and simple bedside maneuvers; imaging may be unavailable.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive weakness of elbow extension with worsening pain
Signs of compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, tense swelling, paresthesia)
Open wound over posterior arm with loss of function
